claim: End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients are at high risk of severe COVID-19.
source: End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients are at high risk of severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: 436 circulating proteins were measured in serial blood samples from hospitalised and non-hospitalised ESKD patients with COVID-19 (n = 256 samples from 55 patients).
source: We measured 436 circulating proteins in serial blood samples from hospitalised and non-hospitalised ESKD patients with COVID-19 (n = 256 samples from 55 patients).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Comparison to 51 non-infected patients revealed 221 differentially expressed proteins.
source: Comparison to 51 non-infected patients revealed 221 differentially expressed proteins, with consistent results in a separate subcohort of 46 COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the differential expression analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity.
source: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity, including IL6, markers of monocyte recruitment (e.g. CCL2, CCL7), neutrophil activation (e.g. proteinase-3), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the severity analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: IL6 is associated with clinical severity of COVID-19.
source: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity, including IL6, markers of monocyte recruitment (e.g. CCL2, CCL7), neutrophil activation (e.g. proteinase-3), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19).
evidence: IL6 is explicitly listed as one of the proteins associated with clinical severity.

claim: CCL2 and CCL7 are markers of monocyte recruitment associated with clinical severity.
source: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity, including IL6, markers of monocyte recruitment (e.g. CCL2, CCL7), neutrophil activation (e.g. proteinase-3), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19).
evidence: CCL2 and CCL7 are explicitly identified as markers of monocyte recruitment associated with severity.

claim: Proteinase-3 is a marker of neutrophil activation associated with clinical severity.
source: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity, including IL6, markers of monocyte recruitment (e.g. CCL2, CCL7), neutrophil activation (e.g. proteinase-3), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19).
evidence: Proteinase-3 is explicitly identified as a marker of neutrophil activation associated with severity.

claim: KRT19 is a marker of epithelial injury associated with clinical severity.
source: Two hundred and three proteins were associated with clinical severity, including IL6, markers of monocyte recruitment (e.g. CCL2, CCL7), neutrophil activation (e.g. proteinase-3), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19).
evidence: KRT19 is explicitly identified as a marker of epithelial injury associated with severity.

claim: Machine-learning identified IL18BP, CTSD, GDF15, and KRT19 as predictors of severity.
source: Machine-learning identified predictors of severity including IL18BP, CTSD, GDF15, and KRT19.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the machine learning analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Survival analysis with joint models revealed 69 predictors of death.
source: Survival analysis with joint models revealed 69 predictors of death.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the survival analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Longitudinal modelling with linear mixed models uncovered 32 proteins displaying different temporal profiles in severe versus non-severe disease.
source: Longitudinal modelling with linear mixed models uncovered 32 proteins displaying different temporal profiles in severe versus non-severe disease, including integrins and adhesion molecules.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the longitudinal analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Integrins and adhesion molecules display different temporal profiles in severe versus non-severe disease.
source: Longitudinal modelling with linear mixed models uncovered 32 proteins displaying different temporal profiles in severe versus non-severe disease, including integrins and adhesion molecules.
evidence: Integrins and adhesion molecules are explicitly mentioned as examples of proteins with different temporal profiles.

claim: Epithelial damage is implicated in the pathology of severe COVID-19.
source: These data implicate epithelial damage, innate immune activation, and leucocyte–endothelial interactions in the pathology of severe COVID-19 and provide a resource for identifying drug targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Innate immune activation is implicated in the pathology of severe COVID-19.
source: These data implicate epithelial damage, innate immune activation, and leucocyte–endothelial interactions in the pathology of severe COVID-19 and provide a resource for identifying drug targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Leucocyte–endothelial interactions are implicated in the pathology of severe COVID-19.
source: These data implicate epithelial damage, innate immune activation, and leucocyte–endothelial interactions in the pathology of severe COVID-19 and provide a resource for identifying drug targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Dexamethasone was the first treatment shown to reduce mortality from COVID-19 in randomised trials.
source: The first treatment shown to reduce mortality from COVID-19 in randomised trials was dexamethasone (Horby et al., 2020), a corticosteroid that has broad non-specific effects on the immune system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Horby et al., 2020.

claim: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid that has broad non-specific effects on the immune system.
source: The first treatment shown to reduce mortality from COVID-19 in randomised trials was dexamethasone (Horby et al., 2020), a corticosteroid that has broad non-specific effects on the immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dexamethasone.

claim: Even with corticosteroid treatment, mortality in severe COVID-19 remains significant.
source: Even with corticosteroid treatment, mortality in severe COVID-19 remains significant.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction.

claim: The REMAP-CAP trial has demonstrated efficacy of anti-IL6 receptor blockade in patients admitted to intensive care units with severe disease.
source: Recently, the REMAP-CAP trial has demonstrated efficacy of anti-IL6 receptor blockade in patients admitted to intensive care units with severe disease (Gordon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gordon et al., 2021.

claim: Proteins are the effector molecules of biology and the targets of most drugs.
source: Proteins are the effector molecules of biology and the targets of most drugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in biology and pharmacology.

claim: Proteomic profiling to identify the key mediators of severe disease provides a valuable tool for identifying and prioritising potential drug targets.
source: Therefore, proteomic profiling to identify the key mediators of severe disease provides a valuable tool for identifying and prioritising potential drug targets (Suhre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suhre et al., 2021.

claim: Risk factors for severe or fatal COVID-19 include age, male sex, non-European ancestry, obesity, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, and immunosuppression.
source: Risk factors for severe or fatal COVID-19 include age, male sex, non-European ancestry, obesity, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, and immunosuppression (Williamson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Williamson et al., 2020.

claim: End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is one of the strongest risk factors for severe COVID-19 with an estimated hazard ratio for death of 3.69.
source: End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is one of the strongest risk factors for severe COVID-19 (estimated hazard ratio for death 3.69) (Williamson et al., 2020), and ESKD patients hospitalised with COVID-19 have a mortality of approximately 30% (Docherty et al., 2020; Corbett et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2020; Valeri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williamson et al., 2020 and other studies.

claim: ESKD patients hospitalised with COVID-19 have a mortality of approximately 30%.
source: End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is one of the strongest risk factors for severe COVID-19 (estimated hazard ratio for death 3.69) (Williamson et al., 2020), and ESKD patients hospitalised with COVID-19 have a mortality of approximately 30% (Docherty et al., 2020; Corbett et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2020; Valeri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ESKD patients have a high prevalence of vascular and cardiometabolic disease.
source: ESKD patients have a high prevalence of vascular and cardiometabolic disease (e.g. hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, diabetes), either as a result of the underlying cause of their renal disease or as a consequence of renal failure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ESKD patients.

claim: ESKD results in both relative immunosuppression and chronic low-grade inflammation.
source: In addition, ESKD results in both relative immunosuppression and chronic low-grade inflammation, which may impact viral defence and the host inflammatory response.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ESKD.

claim: The study performed proteomic profiling of serial blood samples of ESKD patients with COVID-19.
source: Here we performed proteomic profiling of serial blood samples of ESKD patients with COVID-19, leveraging the unique opportunity for longitudinal sampling in both the outpatient and inpatient settings afforded by a large multi-ethnic haemodialysis cohort (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the study design and references Figure 1a.

claim: The study leveraged the unique opportunity for longitudinal sampling in both the outpatient and inpatient settings afforded by a large multi-ethnic haemodialysis cohort.
source: Here we performed proteomic profiling of serial blood samples of ESKD patients with COVID-19, leveraging the unique opportunity for longitudinal sampling in both the outpatient and inpatient settings afforded by a large multi-ethnic haemodialysis cohort (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the study design.

claim: The data revealed 221 proteins that are dysregulated in COVID-19 versus matched non-infected ESKD patients.
source: These data revealed 221 proteins that are dysregulated in COVID-19 versus matched non-infected ESKD patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Using linear mixed models, joint models, and machine learning, the study identified proteins that are markers of COVID-19 severity and risk of death.
source: Using linear mixed models, joint models, and machine learning, we identified proteins that are markers of COVID-19 severity and risk of death.
evidence: This describes the analytical methods and findings.

claim: The study characterised the temporal dynamics of the blood proteomic response during COVID-19 infection in ESKD patients.
source: Finally, we characterised the temporal dynamics of the blood proteomic response during COVID-19 infection in ESKD patients, uncovering 32 proteins that display altered trajectories in patients with severe versus non-severe disease.
evidence: This describes a key finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: 55 ESKD patients with COVID-19 were recruited for subcohort A.
source: We recruited 55 ESKD patients with COVID-19 (subcohort A; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the sample size for subcohort A.

claim: All patients in subcohort A were receiving haemodialysis prior to acquiring COVID-19.
source: All patients were receiving haemodialysis prior to acquiring COVID-19.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the study population.

claim: At time of initial sample, 30 patients were outpatients attending haemodialysis sessions and 25 were hospitalised inpatients.
source: At time of initial sample, 30 patients were outpatients attending haemodialysis sessions and 25 were hospitalised inpatients (see Materials and methods, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the clinical status of patients at the time of initial sampling.

claim: Serial sampling was performed for 51/55 patients following the initial blood sample.
source: Following the initial blood sample, serial sampling was performed for 51/55 patients.
evidence: This describes the longitudinal sampling strategy.

claim: 51 non-infected haemodialysis patients were recruited as ESKD controls.
source: We also recruited 51 non-infected haemodialysis patients as ESKD controls, mirroring the age, sex, and ethnicity distribution of the COVID-19 cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This describes the control group for the study.

claim: The Olink proteomics platform was used to measure 436 proteins in 256 plasma samples from the COVID-19 patients and the 51 control samples.
source: We used the Olink proteomics platform to measure 436 proteins (Supplementary file 1a) in 256 plasma samples from the COVID-19 patients and the 51 control samples.
evidence: This describes the proteomic assay method and sample numbers.

claim: The 436 proteins assayed showed strong enrichment for immune-related proteins.
source: The 436 proteins assayed showed strong enrichment for immune-related proteins (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the protein panel used.

claim: The proteins measured consisted of five multiplex 'panels' focussed on proteins relevant to immuno-inflammation, cardiovascular, and cardiometabolic disease.
source: The proteins measured consisted of five multiplex 'panels' focussed on proteins relevant to immuno-inflammation, cardiovascular, and cardiometabolic disease.
evidence: This describes the composition of the proteomic assay.

claim: 27 of 55 (49.1%) patients in subcohort A had severe or critical disease.
source: Twenty-seven of 55 (49.1%) patients had severe or critical disease (defined by peak WHO severity).
evidence: This describes the clinical severity distribution in subcohort A.

claim: Nine (16.4%) patients in subcohort A died.
source: Nine (16.4%) patients died.
evidence: This describes the mortality rate in subcohort A.

claim: For subcohort B, blood was collected in serum tubes.
source: For these patients, blood was collected in serum tubes and centrifuged to obtain serum.
evidence: This describes the sample type for subcohort B.

claim: 41 of 46 patients in subcohort B were inpatients.
source: Five were outpatients and 41 were inpatients, reflecting the fact that UK policy was weighted towards inpatient testing at the time these patients were recruited.
evidence: This describes the clinical status of patients in subcohort B.

claim: 33 of 46 patients (71.7%) in subcohort B had severe or critical disease.
source: Thirty-three of 46 patients (71.7%) had severe or critical disease (by peak WHO severity), and nine (19.6%) patients died.
evidence: This describes the clinical severity distribution in subcohort B.

claim: Nine (19.6%) patients in subcohort B died.
source: Thirty-three of 46 patients (71.7%) had severe or critical disease (by peak WHO severity), and nine (19.6%) patients died.
evidence: This describes the mortality rate in subcohort B.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of proteomic data from subcohort A demonstrated differences between samples from COVID-19-positive cases and controls.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of proteomic data from subcohort A demonstrated differences between samples from COVID-19-positive cases and controls, although the two groups did not separate into discrete clusters (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This describes a finding from the PCA analysis and references Figure 2.

claim: The two groups (COVID-19-positive cases and controls) did not separate into discrete clusters in PCA.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of proteomic data from subcohort A demonstrated differences between samples from COVID-19-positive cases and controls, although the two groups did not separate into discrete clusters (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This describes a finding from the PCA analysis.

claim: Differential expression analysis in subcohort A revealed 221 proteins associated with COVID-19 at 5% FDR.
source: This revealed 221 proteins associated with COVID-19 (5% false discovery rate, FDR); the vast majority were upregulated, with only 40 downregulated (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: The vast majority of proteins associated with COVID-19 were upregulated, with only 40 downregulated.
source: This revealed 221 proteins associated with COVID-19 (5% false discovery rate, FDR); the vast majority were upregulated, with only 40 downregulated (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This describes the directionality of protein changes in COVID-19.

claim: The most strongly upregulated proteins (in terms of fold change) were DDX58, CCL7, IL6, CXCL11, KRT19, and CXCL10.
source: The most strongly upregulated proteins (in terms of fold change) were DDX58, CCL7, IL6, CXCL11, KRT19, and CXCL10, and the most strongly downregulated were SERPINA5, CCL16, FABP2, PON3, ITGA11, and MMP12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the proteins with the largest fold changes.

claim: The most strongly downregulated proteins were SERPINA5, CCL16, FABP2, PON3, ITGA11, and MMP12.
source: The most strongly upregulated proteins (in terms of fold change) were DDX58, CCL7, IL6, CXCL11, KRT19, and CXCL10, and the most strongly downregulated were SERPINA5, CCL16, FABP2, PON3, ITGA11, and MMP12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the proteins with the largest fold changes.

claim: Many of the upregulated proteins were chemotaxins.
source: Notably, many of the upregulated proteins were chemotaxins.
evidence: This is an observation about the functional categories of upregulated proteins.

claim: Testing for associations between proteins and clinical severity within COVID-19-positive cases from subcohort A revealed 203 proteins associated with severity.
source: This analysis revealed 203 proteins associated with severity (Figure 3b, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the severity analysis.

claim: The majority of proteins associated with severity were upregulated in more severe disease, with only 42 downregulated.
source: The majority of these were upregulated in more severe disease, with only 42 downregulated.
evidence: This describes the directionality of protein changes with severity.

claim: Severe COVID-19 was characterised by elevated IL6.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that severe COVID-19 was characterised by elevated IL6.
evidence: This finding is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Severe COVID-19 was characterised by a signature of upregulated monocyte chemokines (e.g. CCL2, CCL7, CXCL10).
source: In addition, we observed a signature of upregulated monocyte chemokines (e.g. CCL2, CCL7, CXCL10), neutrophil activation and degranulation (e.g. PRTN3, MPO), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19, AREG, PSIP1, GRN). (Figures 3b,c and 5).
evidence: This describes a key finding about the proteomic signature of severe COVID-19.

claim: Severe COVID-19 was characterised by neutrophil activation and degranulation (e.g. PRTN3, MPO).
source: In addition, we observed a signature of upregulated monocyte chemokines (e.g. CCL2, CCL7, CXCL10), neutrophil activation and degranulation (e.g. PRTN3, MPO), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19, AREG, PSIP1, GRN). (Figures 3b,c and 5).
evidence: This describes a key finding about the proteomic signature of severe COVID-19.

claim: Severe COVID-19 was characterised by epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19, AREG, PSIP1, GRN).
source: In addition, we observed a signature of upregulated monocyte chemokines (e.g. CCL2, CCL7, CXCL10), neutrophil activation and degranulation (e.g. PRTN3, MPO), and epithelial injury (e.g. KRT19, AREG, PSIP1, GRN). (Figures 3b,c and 5).
evidence: This describes a key finding about the proteomic signature of severe COVID-19.

claim: SERPINA5 and leptin showed the greatest downregulation as COVID-19 severity increased.
source: SERPINA5 and leptin showed the greatest downregulation as COVID-19 severity increased (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This describes proteins with the greatest downregulation with severity.

claim: The majority (140/203; 69%) of severity-associated proteins were also identified as differentially abundant in the COVID-19-positive versus -negative analysis.
source: The majority (140/203; 69%) of severity-associated proteins were also identified as differentially abundant in the COVID-19-positive versus -negative analysis (Figure 6a).
evidence: This describes the overlap between two analyses.

claim: Log fold changes for proteins in COVID-19 versus non-infected patients were correlated with effect sizes in the severity analysis.
source: Log fold changes for proteins in COVID-19 versus non-infected patients were correlated with effect sizes in the severity analysis, such that the proteins most upregulated in cases versus controls also tended to show the greatest upregulation in severe disease (Figure 6b).
evidence: This describes a correlation between two analyses.

claim: CCL20, IL17C, and OSM were strongly associated with severity, but not differentially expressed in infected versus non-infected patients.
source: However, there were some notable exceptions (e.g. CCL20, IL17C, OSM) that were strongly associated with severity, but not differentially expressed in infected versus non-infected patients (Figure 6c).
evidence: This describes proteins specifically associated with severity.

claim: PCA revealed that some samples from patients who had mild or moderate disease at the time of sampling clustered with samples from patients with severe disease.
source: PCA revealed that some samples from patients who had mild or moderate disease at the time of sampling clustered with samples from patients with severe disease (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis.

claim: Samples that clustered with severe disease came from individuals who subsequently developed severe or critical disease.
source: Examination of the same PCA plot labelling samples according to the patient's overall clinical course (measured by peak WHO severity score over the duration of the illness) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) revealed that these samples came from individuals who subsequently developed severe or critical disease.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis suggesting predictive value.

claim: Molecular changes may predate clinical deterioration.
source: This suggested that molecular changes may predate clinical deterioration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA analysis.

claim: The Random Forests method achieved 71% accuracy in predicting peak severity using proteomic predictors.
source: The Random Forests method achieved 71% accuracy in predicting peak severity.
evidence: This is a result from the machine learning analysis.

claim: Using only clinically available predictors, the Random Forests method achieved 66% accuracy in predicting peak severity.
source: By contrast, using only clinically available predictors (demographics, comorbidities, and clinical laboratory results), the Random Forests method achieved 66% accuracy in predicting peak severity.
evidence: This is a result from the machine learning analysis.

claim: Combining clinical parameters plus proteins did not improve accuracy (71%) compared to using proteomic predictors alone.
source: Combining clinical parameters plus proteins did not improve accuracy (71%) compared to using proteomic predictors alone, suggesting that the information contained in the clinical predictors is captured at the proteomic level.
evidence: This is a result from the machine learning analysis.

claim: The information contained in the clinical predictors is captured at the proteomic level.
source: Combining clinical parameters plus proteins did not improve accuracy (71%) compared to using proteomic predictors alone, suggesting that the information contained in the clinical predictors is captured at the proteomic level.
evidence: This is an inference from the machine learning results.

claim: The most important proteins for indicating the presence of current or future severe disease were IL18BP, CTSD (Cathepsin D), GDF15, KRT19, TNFSF11, and IL1RL1 (ST2).
source: The most important proteins for indicating the presence of current or future severe disease were IL18BP, CTSD (Cathepsin D), GDF15, KRT19, TNFSF11, and IL1RL1 (ST2) (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a result from the feature importance analysis of the Random Forests model.

claim: KRT19 emerged as a key biomarker of severe disease through the Random Forests analytical approach.
source: It is notable that through this distinct analytical approach, KRT19 again emerged as a key biomarker of severe disease.
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of findings across different analytical methods.

claim: Nine of 55 patients in subcohort A died.
source: Nine of 55 patients in subcohort A died.
evidence: This describes the mortality in subcohort A.

claim: Joint models identified 44 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with increased risk of death.
source: This analysis identified 44 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with increased risk of death (Figure 7b, Supplementary file 1f), including CST3, IL22RA1, AZU1, CCL28, and SPON1, and 25 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with reduced risk of death, including CD84, TNFSF12, TANK, PRKCQ, and ADM.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the survival analysis.

claim: Joint models identified 25 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with reduced risk of death.
source: This analysis identified 44 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with increased risk of death (Figure 7b, Supplementary file 1f), including CST3, IL22RA1, AZU1, CCL28, and SPON1, and 25 proteins for which increased concentration was associated with reduced risk of death, including CD84, TNFSF12, TANK, PRKCQ, and ADM.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the survival analysis.

claim: Associations were found between plasma proteins and all clinical laboratory measurements except troponin.
source: We found associations between plasma proteins and all clinical laboratory measurements except troponin (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This describes findings from the analysis of protein associations with clinical lab tests.

claim: Many proteins associated with clinical laboratory measurements were also markers of severity.
source: Many of these proteins were also markers of severity (e.g. IL6, KRT19, IFN-gamma, and CXCL10 were strongly associated with raised CRP and ferritin and reduced lymphocyte counts).
evidence: This describes overlap between proteins associated with lab tests and severity.

claim: CCL7 was associated with lower monocyte count and raised inflammatory markers.
source: Of note, CCL7, a monocyte chemokine that was also identified as an important marker of severity by the Random Forests classifier, was associated with lower monocyte count and raised inflammatory markers.
evidence: This describes a specific finding about CCL7.

claim: Elevated neutrophil count was associated with Oncostatin-M, MMP9, and defensin.
source: Elevated neutrophil count was associated with Oncostatin-M, which regulates IL6, GCSF, and GMCSF production, and with the proteases MMP9 and defensin.
evidence: This describes associations between neutrophil count and specific proteins.

claim: One hundred and seventy-eight proteins displayed a significant association with time from first symptoms (5% FDR).
source: One hundred and seventy-eight proteins displayed a significant association with time from first symptoms (5% FDR), demonstrating the temporal variability in plasma proteins across the disease course (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: 32 proteins displayed significant interaction between time and severity, showing differential temporal trajectories between mild/moderate and severe/critical infections.
source: Moreover, we identified 32 proteins for which there was significant interaction between time and severity, that is, proteins displaying differential temporal trajectories between mild/moderate and severe/critical infections (Supplementary file 1h, Figure 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: Among the proteins with the strongest temporal differences according to clinical course were the integrins ITGA11 and ITGB6, the adhesion molecule ICAM1, TNFRSF10B (a receptor for TRAIL), and PLAUR (the receptor for urokinase plasminogen activator).
source: Among the proteins with the strongest temporal differences according to clinical course were the integrins ITGA11 and ITGB6, the adhesion molecule ICAM1, TNFRSF10B (a receptor for TRAIL), and PLAUR (the receptor for urokinase plasminogen activator).
evidence: This describes proteins with the strongest temporal differences.

claim: Most proteins with temporal differences exhibited rising profiles in the more severe patients but flat profiles in milder cases.
source: Most of these proteins exhibited rising profiles in the more severe patients but flat profiles in milder cases.
evidence: This describes a pattern in the temporal trajectories.

claim: ACE2, the receptor for SARS-CoV-2, displayed rising profiles in severe patients but flat profiles in milder cases.
source: ACE2, the receptor for SARS-CoV-2, also displayed this pattern (Figure 9).
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of ACE2.

claim: ITGA11 abundance fell over time in the severe group.
source: In contrast, abundance of ITGA11, which was also identified as reduced in the analysis of infected versus non-infected patients, fell over time in the severe group.
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of ITGA11.

claim: In COVID-19-negative ESKD patients, no proteins were significantly associated with ethnicity in a multivariable model adjusting for age and sex.
source: In COVID-19-negative ESKD patients, no proteins were significantly associated with ethnicity in a multivariable model adjusting for age and sex.
evidence: This is a finding from the ethnicity analysis.

claim: In COVID-19-positive ESKD patients, a single protein, LY75, was associated with ethnicity in a multivariable model (nominal p-value 0.0001, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value 0.04, with higher levels in white patients).
source: In COVID-19-positive ESKD patients, there is the potential for protein associations with ethnicity to be confounded by disease severity. To account for this, we included severity as well as age and sex as covariates. A single protein, LY75, was associated with ethnicity in this multivariable model (nominal p-value 0.0001, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value 0.04, with higher levels in white patients).
evidence: This is a finding from the ethnicity analysis.

claim: Using the same within-case analysis strategy in subcohort B, no proteins were significantly associated with ethnicity after multiple testing correction.
source: Using the same within-case analysis strategy in subcohort B, we found no proteins were significantly associated with ethnicity after multiple testing correction, although the nominal p-value for LY75 was 0.025.
evidence: This is a finding from the ethnicity analysis in subcohort B.

claim: Of the 221 proteins that were differentially abundant in the analysis of COVID-19-positive versus -negative ESKD patients, 116 associations had been previously reported.
source: Of the 221 proteins that were differentially abundant in our analysis of COVID-19-positive versus -negative ESKD patients, 116 associations had been previously reported (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This describes the overlap with previous studies.

claim: Of the 203 proteins associated with severity, 165 had previously been reported.
source: Of the 203 proteins associated with severity, 165 had previously been reported (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This describes the overlap with previous studies.

claim: Of the 221 proteins differentially abundant in the case/control analysis, 210 were measured in the Filbin et al., 2020 study.
source: Of the 221 proteins differentially abundant in our case/control analysis, 210 were measured in their study.
evidence: This describes the overlap in proteins measured between studies.

claim: Of the 210 proteins measured in both studies, 100 (47.6%) were significant in the Filbin et al., 2020 analysis of COVID-19-positive versus COVID-19-negative respiratory distress.
source: Of these, 100 (47.6%) were significant in their analysis of COVID-19-positive versus COVID-19-negative respiratory distress.
evidence: This describes the concordance with the Filbin et al., 2020 study.

claim: Strong correlation (r = 0.69) was observed between the estimated log fold changes in this study and the Filbin et al., 2020 study.
source: In addition, we observed strong correlation (r = 0.69) between the estimated log fold changes in our and their studies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the correlation with the Filbin et al., 2020 study.

claim: Of the 203 proteins associated with severity in this study, 192 were measured in the Filbin et al., 2020 study.
source: Of the 203 proteins associated with severity in our study, 192 were measured in their study.
evidence: This describes the overlap in proteins measured between studies.

claim: One hundred and fifty-seven of the 192 proteins were significantly associated with severity in the Filbin et al., 2020 study, giving a concordance of 81.8%.
source: One hundred and fifty-seven of these were significantly associated with severity, giving a concordance of 81.8%.
evidence: This describes the concordance with the Filbin et al., 2020 study.

claim: Despite differences in study design and clinical populations, notable similarities were observed between this study's results and those reported by Filbin et al., 2020.
source: Thus, despite the differences in study design and clinical populations, we observed notable similarities in our results and those reported by Filbin et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the comparison with the Filbin et al., 2020 study.

claim: A strength of the study was the ability to perform serial blood sampling in both the outpatient and inpatient settings.
source: A strength of our study was that we were able to perform serial blood sampling in both the outpatient and inpatient settings, including longitudinal samples from the same individual before and after hospitalisation.
evidence: This describes a strength of the study design.

claim: Serial blood sampling was possible because haemodialysis patients must continue to attend for regular dialysis sessions and are unable to fully isolate.
source: This was possible because haemodialysis patients are unable to fully isolate as they must continue to attend for regular dialysis sessions.
evidence: This explains why serial sampling was feasible in this population.

claim: Data from the UK Renal Registry shows that 7 and 14 day mortality for COVID-19-infected in-centre haemodialysis patients was 11% and 19%, respectively.
source: Data from the UK Renal Registry shows that 7 and 14 day mortality for COVID-19-infected in-centre haemodialysis patients was 11% and 19%, respectively (COVID-19 Data, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the UK Renal Registry.

claim: Data from the Scottish Renal Registry estimates 30 day mortality following a positive COVID-19 test as 22%.

source: For serum, the median correlation between the assays was 0.991 with an IQR of 0.952–0.995 and a range of 0.737–0.999.
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of duplicate assays in serum.

claim: Duplicate assays were removed at random prior to subsequent analyses.
source: We removed duplicate assays at random prior to subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes the handling of duplicate measurements.

claim: For 11 ESKD controls, contemporaneous plasma and serum samples were available.
source: For 11 ESKD controls, we had contemporaneous plasma and serum samples.
evidence: This describes the availability of paired samples.

claim: 344 of 436 (78.9%) proteins had a Pearson's r > 0.5 between plasma and serum assays.
source: Three hundred and forty-four of 436 (78.9%) proteins had a Pearson's r > 0.5.
evidence: This describes the correlation between plasma and serum measurements.

claim: Following QC, 0.22% data points were missing for the plasma dataset and 0.35% for the serum dataset.
source: Following QC, 0.22% data points were missing for the plasma dataset and 0.35% for the serum dataset.
evidence: This describes the extent of missing data.

claim: For analyses that required no missing values (PCA and supervised learning), missing values were imputed using caret's k-nearest neighbours method.
source: For analyses that required no missing values (PCA and supervised learning), we imputed missing values as follows. The dataset was first scaled and centred, and missing values imputed using caret's k-nearest neighbours method (Kuhn, 2008).
evidence: This describes the imputation method for missing values.

claim: The five closest samples (by Euclidean distance) were used to estimate each missing value.
source: The five closest samples (by Euclidean distance) were used to estimate each missing value.
evidence: This describes the parameters of the imputation method.

claim: Singular value decomposition was used to perform PCA on the proteomic data from subcohort A (plasma samples).
source: Singular value decomposition was used to perform PCA on the proteomic data from subcohort A (plasma samples).
evidence: This describes the PCA method.

claim: The loadings from subcohort A were used together with the proteomic data from subcohort B to calculate principal component scores, enabling projection of subcohort B data into the PCA space of subcohort A.
source: We then used the loadings from subcohort A together with the proteomic data from subcohort B to calculate principal component scores. This enabled projection of subcohort B data into the PCA space of subcohort A.
evidence: This describes the method for projecting subcohort B into the PCA space.

claim: Linear mixed models were used for differential protein abundance analyses to account for the use of serial samples from the same individuals.
source: Differential protein abundance analyses between COVID-19 positive and negative samples were performed using linear mixed models, to account for the use of serial samples from the same individuals (R lme4 package Bates et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: Age, sex, and ethnicity were included as covariates in the differential abundance analysis.
source: Age, sex, and ethnicity were included as covariates.
evidence: This describes the covariates included in the analysis.

claim: A random intercept term was used to estimate the variability between individuals in the study and account for repeated measures.
source: We used a random intercept term to estimate the variability between individuals in the study and account for repeated measures.
evidence: This describes the random effects structure of the model.

claim: P-values were calculated using a type 3 F-test in conjunction with Satterthwaite's method for estimating the degrees of freedom for fixed effects.
source: We calculated P-values using a type 3 F-test in conjunction with Satterthwaite's method for estimating the degrees of freedom for fixed effects (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating p-values.

claim: The regression model was fitted for each of the 436 proteins individually.
source: The regression model was fitted for each of the 436 proteins individually.
evidence: This describes the approach to testing multiple proteins.

claim: Multiple testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method and a 5% FDR used for the significance threshold.
source: Multiple testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method and a 5% FDR used for the significance threshold.
evidence: This describes the multiple testing correction method.

claim: For testing the association of plasma proteins with the four-level WHO severity rating within COVID-19-positive cases, the covid_status term was replaced by a severity variable encoded using orthogonal polynomial contrasts to account for ordinal nature of severity levels.
source: For testing the association of plasma proteins with the four-level WHO severity rating (mild, moderate, severe, and critical) within COVID-19-positive cases from subcohort A (n = 256 samples from 55 patients), we used a similar linear mixed modelling approach to the COVID-19-positive versus -negative differential abundance analysis; for this analysis, the covid_status term was replaced by a severity variable encoded using orthogonal polynomial contrasts to account for ordinal nature of severity levels.
evidence: This describes the method for testing associations with severity.

claim: The linear mixed modelling strategy was employed for testing association of temporal clinical laboratory variables and protein levels.
source: The linear mixed modelling strategy was also employed for testing association of temporal clinical laboratory variables and protein levels, with the value of the clinical variable (as a quantitative trait) used in place of covid_status.
evidence: This describes the method for testing associations with clinical lab variables.

claim: Only COVID-19-positive patients were included in the analysis of associations with clinical laboratory variables.
source: Only COVID-19-positive patients were included in this analysis.
evidence: This describes the sample for the clinical lab analysis.

claim: Correlations between clinical laboratory variables and protein levels were calculated using the R package rmcorr.
source: We also calculated correlations between clinical laboratory variables and protein levels using the R package rmcorr, which determines the overall within-individual relationship among paired measures that have been taken on two or more occasion (Bakdash and Marusich, 2017).
evidence: This describes an additional method for analyzing associations with clinical lab variables.

claim: Testing of protein levels and ethnicity was performed separately in COVID-19-negative ESKD patients and COVID-19-positive ESKD patients.
source: We performed testing of protein levels and ethnicity separately in COVID-19-negative ESKD patients and COVID-19-positive ESKD patients.
evidence: This describes the approach to testing associations with ethnicity.

claim: The Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the FDR at 5% for all statistical analyses.
source: We used the Benjamini–Hochberg method to control the FDR at 5% for all statistical analyses.
evidence: This describes the multiple testing correction approach.

claim: The plug-in procedure was used as an alternative method to estimate the FDR.
source: To provide additional support that the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure was providing adequate control of the FDR, we also used the plug-in procedure (Hastie et al., 2001) as an alternative method to estimate the FDR, as described below.
evidence: This describes an additional method for FDR estimation.

claim: Using the plug-in method, the estimated FDR for the case versus control analysis was 0.062 and for the severity analysis 0.057.
source: Using this method, the estimated FDR for the case versus control analysis was 0.062 and for the severity analysis 0.057, indicating that we had appropriately controlled the FDR.
evidence: This is a result from the alternative FDR estimation method.

claim: 100,000 permutations of the case–control labels were used to estimate the null distribution for calculating empirical p-values.
source: We again used 100,000 permutations of the case–control labels to estimate the null distribution.
evidence: This describes the permutation approach for empirical p-value calculation.

claim: On no occasion in 100,000 permutations did the number of proteins declared significant exceed the number in the real data for the case-control analysis.
source: The distribution of the number of proteins declared significant is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a; on no occasion in 100,000 permutations did we observe more proteins declared significant than in the real data.
evidence: This is a result from the permutation analysis.

claim: The empirical p-value for the case-control analysis is less than 1×10−5.
source: We can thus state that the empirical p-value (the fraction of permutation runs where we observed ≥ the number of associations in the real data) is less than 1/100,000 = 1×10−5.
evidence: This is a result from the permutation analysis.

claim: On no occasion in 100,000 permutations did the number of proteins declared significant exceed the number in the real data for the severity analysis.
source: Again, on no occasion in 100,000 permutations did we observe more proteins declared significant than in the real data (empirical p-value<1×10−5).
evidence: This is a result from the permutation analysis for the severity analysis.

claim: Random forest models were fitted using R's randomForest and caret packages.
source: Random forest models were fitted using R's randomForest and caret packages (Kuhn, 2008; Leo, 2001).
evidence: This describes the software used for machine learning.

claim: Fourfold cross-validation was used to estimate model accuracy, repeated 100 times.
source: To estimate model accuracy, we used fourfold cross-validation. The cross-validation procedure was repeated 100 times.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation approach.

claim: The model's parameters were kept constant at 500 trees and an mtry value calculated as the square root of the number of features.
source: The model's parameters were kept constant at 500 trees and an mtry value (number of proteins randomly sampled as candidates at each node) calculated as the square root of the number of features.
evidence: This describes the Random Forests parameters.

claim: After parameter estimation, a final model was fitted trained using the entirety of the dataset.
source: After parameter estimation, we fitted a final model trained using the entirety of the dataset.
evidence: This describes the final model training.

claim: Random forest feature extraction was carried out using the R randomForestExplainer package.
source: Random forest feature extraction was carried out using the R randomForestExplainer package.
evidence: This describes the software used for feature extraction.

claim: Linear mixed models were fitted for each protein to capture the temporal trajectories of each individual, using a polynomial spline of degree two.
source: Following scaling and centring, we fitted linear mixed models for each protein to capture the temporal trajectories of each individual. A polynomial spline of degree two was used to model protein concentration with respect to time (from symptom onset, measured in days); the spline was fitted for samples that were taken between 1 and 28 days from first symptoms, inclusive.
evidence: This describes the method for modeling temporal trajectories in the survival analysis.

claim: Linear mixed models were joined to a Cox regression model using the jointModel package.
source: These were joined to a Cox regression model using the jointModel package (Rizopoulos, 2010) in order to estimate the association of each protein with risk for death.
evidence: This describes the method for joint modeling.

claim: P-values for the joint model were calculated using a Wald test for the association between the linear mixed model and Cox regression.
source: P-values were calculated using a Wald test for the association between the linear mixed model and Cox regression.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating p-values in the joint model.

claim: For the longitudinal analysis, patients were binarised into severe or non-severe clinical course according to the peak WHO severity disease of their illness.
source: For the purposes of this analysis, we binarised patients into severe or non-severe clinical course according to the peak WHO severity disease of their illness.
evidence: This describes the categorization of patients for the longitudinal analysis.

claim: Patients with a peak WHO score of mild or moderate were considered non-severe and those with a peak score of severe or critical were considered severe.
source: Patients with a peak WHO score of mild or moderate were considered non-severe and those with a peak score of severe or critical were considered severe.
evidence: This describes the definition of severe vs non-severe for the longitudinal analysis.

claim: R's bs function was used to fit a polynomial spline of degree two to model protein concentration with respect time in the longitudinal analysis.
source: We then used R's bs function to fit a polynomial spline of degree two to model protein concentration with respect time (from symptom onset, measured in days) (Perperoglou et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the method for modeling temporal trajectories in the longitudinal analysis.

claim: The spline in the longitudinal analysis was fitted for samples that were taken between 1 and 21 days from symptom onset, inclusive.
source: The spline was fitted for samples that were taken between 1 and 21 days from symptom onset, inclusive.
evidence: This describes the time window for the longitudinal analysis.

claim: Random slopes with respect to time, in addition to random intercepts, were estimated to account for each individual's unique disease course in the longitudinal analysis.
source: We estimated random slopes with respect to time, in addition to random intercepts, to account for each individual's unique disease course.
evidence: This describes the random effects structure for the longitudinal analysis.

claim: To identify proteins that changed significantly over time, the p-values for the main effect of time were examined.
source: To identify proteins that changed significantly over time, we examined the p-values for the main effect of time.
evidence: This describes the approach to identifying temporally variable proteins.

claim: To identify proteins with distinct temporal profiles between severe and non-severe cases, the p-values for the time × severity interaction term were examined.
source: To identify proteins with distinct temporal profiles between severe and non-severe cases, we examined the p-values for the time × severity interaction term.
evidence: This describes the approach to identifying proteins with differential temporal trajectories.
